rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate all eight peaks while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Halve the gradient slope while holding the solvent window and temperature fixed to identify which close pairs respond to slope. The first run's early elution suggests this diagnostic should still finish near ten minutes.
Keep the improved slope and test a substantial temperature increase to shift selectivity at the remaining close pair. Higher temperature should also preserve room under the ten-minute time threshold.

Back off temperature by one step to separate the late pair that approaches co-elution at 60 C, while retaining most of the temperature-induced improvement in the central cluster. The last peak should remain comfortably below ten minutes.

At 60 C, test a slightly steeper gradient to move the remaining late close pair away from its apparent slope-dependent crossing. This also shortens the run, while checking whether the central pair retains adequate resolution.

Raise the starting organic fraction slightly while preserving injection 5's gradient slope to fine-tune selectivity at the nearly resolved central pair. This should also shorten retention without pushing the first peak into the unretained region.

Use a slope between the recent trials to improve the central pairs while preserving the late pair's separation gained at phi0 = 0.10. The narrower endpoint remains above the observed elution window, so all peaks should elute within ten minutes.

Reduce the slope slightly from injection 7 to lift both central pairs above R = 1.5 while keeping the late close pair resolved. The endpoint remains well above the last peak's estimated elution composition, with completion expected around 7.5 minutes.

Injection 8 reaches the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark while testing a shorter fully resolved separation. Raise phi0 to reduce retention and simultaneously soften the slope to help preserve the critical central resolutions.

Make the gradient shallower at the higher starting composition to recover the central pair lost in injection 9. This tests whether a fully resolved method can finish sooner than injection 8, which remains the maximum-score benchmark.

The high-temperature optimum has little resolution margin, so test the unexplored low-temperature selectivity regime at a similar slope. The higher starting fraction should offset some added retention; injection 8 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Increase temperature one step to test whether the remaining central pair separates in this lower-temperature elution order. Holding the gradient fixed isolates temperature selectivity and should shorten the run.

At 25 C, test a slightly shallower gradient to open the central close pair while retaining the larger gap ahead of it. This explores an alternative fully resolved region; injection 8 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Shift the fully resolving gradient from injection 13 upward while preserving its slope to remove time spent below the elution window. This should bring the last peak below ten minutes and test whether the low-temperature separation tolerates a higher starting fraction.

Test whether a larger starting-fraction shift carries the central pair through its apparent selectivity crossing into a faster resolved elution order. This is exploratory; injection 8 already secures the maximum CRF.
Shorten the fully resolved method from injection 15 by one gradient-time step. Its minimum resolution of 1.85 provides some margin to compress the separation while preserving the maximum CRF.

Test the next shorter gradient to locate the resolution limit of this fast, maximum-score region. If a critical pair falls below 1.5, injection 16 remains the shortest fully resolved method demonstrated so far.

Return to injection 16's resolving slope but raise the starting fraction one step to shorten retention through a different route. This tests whether the critical pairs tolerate shifting the gradient window upward.

Test a temperature-driven selectivity change at the faster starting composition, aiming to move the central close pair through its crossing. Injection 16 remains the shortest demonstrated fully resolved method if this higher-temperature trial loses resolution elsewhere.

Raise temperature another step to move the central pair farther beyond its crossing, while halving the slope to protect the compressed early pairs. This tests a potentially faster fully resolved alternative to injection 16.

Lower the starting fraction from injection 19 to spread the compressed early cluster, with a gentler slope to support resolution. This tests whether the intermediate-temperature region can deliver full resolution faster than injection 16's 4.14-minute separation.

Test a lower starting fraction to restore central-pair separation, offsetting its added retention with a steeper gradient and modest heating. Injection 16 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Return to 25 C to improve central selectivity, using a steeper gradient to offset the lower starting fraction. This targets a fully resolved separation near or below injection 16's 4.14-minute finish.

Refine around the fast, fully resolved injection 16 with a slightly shallower slope to increase its critical-pair margins. This targets a more robust maximum-score method with only a small retention-time increase.

Trim injection 16's gradient to a shorter programmed window while preserving its resolving slope. The last peak previously eluted at approximately 0.525 organic fraction, so the 0.55 endpoint should retain full resolution and the maximum CRF.
